Name: Ai (et-Tell) (העי (א-תל))
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Ai (et-Tell), dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Amman (Rabbath Ammon) (עמאן (רבת עמון))
Description: A large rock-cut cruciform water reservoir, similar to those at Beit Shemesh and Beersheba, located north of the acropolis. It has an estimated capacity of 1264 cubic meters and features an external opening for water entry and a stepped tunnel for drawing water, dated to Iron Age II. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II with a monumental water system, specifically mentioning a cruciform-shaped reservoir designed to maximize storage volume and prevent roof collapse. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Amman during the Iron Age II.

Name: Arbailu (Erbil) (ארבילו (אירביל))
Description: Sennacherib built an aqueduct to Arbela, starting from the Chai fortress about 20km away. It began with a subterranean tunnel, 1.2m high and 1.12m wide, lined with ashlar stones and featuring shafts every 42m, bringing water from three rivers and springs to the city center. An aqueduct bringing water from a distance outside the city was found at Erbil, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Athens (Acropolis) (אתונה (יוון))
Description: A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Athens, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Baal-Meon (בעלמען)
Description: The Mesha Stele records King Mesha of Moab building the city of Baal-Meon and constructing a water reservoir ('ashuah') or capturing a spring, possibly utilizing Israelite captives for their hydrological knowledge and labor.

Name: Bor Hamat (בור חמת)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, with a volume of approximately 1250 cubic meters.

Name: Buqei'a (Judean Desert) (בקעת הורקניה (בוקיעה))
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Buqei'a, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Gibeon (el-Jib) (גבעון (אל-ג'יב))
Description: A system comprising a horizontal tunnel from a spring to a collection chamber, and a 52m long stepped tunnel ascending into the fortified city, dated by the author to the 10th or 9th century BCE (early Iron Age II). A large circular stepped shaft, 11.3m in diameter and 24m deep, cut into rock with a spiral staircase, designed to access groundwater. The author dates its construction to the 7th century BCE (late Iron Age II). Mentioned as a site with an underground water system where a pulley could have been used, similar to the one depicted in an Assyrian relief, suggesting a sophisticated water supply during sieges. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with two monumental water systems, likely involving tunnels or shafts to access groundwater within the fortified city. A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Gibeon, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Heshbon (חשבון)
Description: A large rock-cut water pool, 17x17m and 7m deep, with an estimated capacity of 2000 cubic meters, discovered in stratum 17 (9th-8th centuries BCE). It was fed by runoff channels and possibly supplemented by water from the 'Ein Hisban spring. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A reservoir or pool was found at Tel Heshbon, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Horbat Radum (חורבת רדום)
Description: Two depressions, approximately 2m in diameter, were found outside the northern wall of this late Iron Age II fortress. These are identified as likely blocked cisterns that served the fortification. Cisterns or pools were found at Radum, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Horbat Rosh Zayit (חורבת ראש זית)
Description: A rock-cut cistern found within the fortress, designed to collect rainwater runoff from the fortress area, dating to the 10th-9th centuries BCE. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Ras ez-Zeit, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Horbat Shilha (חורבת שילחה)
Description: A bell-shaped, rock-cut cistern (Locus 21) with a 0.85m opening and 1.8m diameter at 1.25m depth, located within a four-room house. Runoff was collected via earth channels. Plaster presence is not reported, but typical for such cisterns. Cisterns or pools were found at Shilha, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Horbat Uza (חורבת עוזה)
Description: A covered drainage channel, constructed with stone slabs and over 20m long, was found in the gate passage of the fortress. It started in the plaza, passed under the threshold, and likely terminated in a rock-cut cistern on the slope. Two depressions outside the southern wall of the fortress are identified as likely blocked cisterns, contributing to the site's water supply during the late Iron Age II. Three large cisterns are located 300m south of the fortress in a wadi. The middle cistern is T-shaped, partially rock-cut and partially built with later barrel vaults, estimated at 400 cubic meters, and features multiple plaster layers (possibly Iron Age I and Herodian).

Name: Ibleam (Khirbet Bel'ameh) (יבלעם (ח'רבת בלעמה))
Description: A rock-cut tunnel, approximately 100m long with steps, leading from the Bir Sinjil spring into the ancient tel, characteristic of Iron Age II water systems. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Ibleam, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Jerusalem (City of David) (ירושלים (עיר דוד))
Description: Hezekiah's Tunnel, a 533m long rock-cut channel, diverted water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam within the city walls, constructed in the late 8th century BCE (late Iron Age II) during King Hezekiah's reign. A large pool (15x15m during the First Temple period) located at the southern end of Hezekiah's Tunnel, serving as the primary reservoir for the diverted Gihon Spring waters within the city. Hezekiah's Tunnel, a 530m long rock-cut tunnel, was constructed in the 8th century BCE (Iron II) to divert water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam inside the city walls, a complex engineering feat involving two teams digging from opposite ends. Warren's Shaft, a natural vertical karstic shaft (13m deep), was accidentally discovered in the 8th century BCE during preparations for Hezekiah's Tunnel, leading to attempts to connect it to the Gihon Spring and integrate it into the water system. Channel IV, an overflow channel originating near the Pool of Siloam and extending to the Kidron Valley, is considered by some scholars to be an original part of Hezekiah's Tunnel, dating its construction to the 8th century BCE. Various pools mentioned in biblical texts (e.g., Upper Pool, Lower Pool, Old Pool, Pool of Siloam) likely collected runoff water, serving as secondary water sources for the city, primarily for non-drinking uses during the Iron Age. The 'Hasmonean Water Channel,' a rock-cut channel near the Temple Mount, collected runoff water for cisterns. Although named Hasmonean, some scholars propose it dates to the First Temple period (Iron Age). Bir Ayub, identified with biblical Ein Rogel, is a 38m deep well fed by a small cave and fissures. Its water was primarily used for irrigating fields and gardens, and its biblical mentions indicate its use during the Iron Age. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. An aqueduct system within the city, likely feeding a reservoir or pool, was present in Jerusalem during the Iron Age II. A reservoir or pool, likely fed by an aqueduct or tunnel, was present in Jerusalem during the Iron Age II.

Name: Jit (ג'ית)
Description: An ancient, rock-cut pool known as 'El-Ein' (the spring), consisting of three parts with a total depth of 13.73m. Its water source is a spring, fed by a 1.5m high tunnel from a hard limestone layer, making it a central water facility.

Name: Kadesh Barnea (Ein el-Gudeirat) (קדש ברנע (עין אל-קודייראת))
Description: A water system in the Middle Fortress (8th-7th centuries BCE) consisting of a stone-built, plastered reservoir (approx. 140 cubic meters) with 25 steps leading to its bottom, fed by a plastered channel from the main spring, Ein Qudeirat. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Kadesh Barnea during the Iron Age II.

Name: Kerem es-Samra (Kerem el-Ajez) (כרם א-סמרא (כרם אל עג'ז))
Description: A large pool measuring 22x18m, located in the southwest of the fortress, with collapsed walls. It served as a water reservoir for the Iron Age II fortress.

Name: Khirbet Abu et-Twein (חורבת אבו א-טווין)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Ibn Tuwayn, dated to the Iron Age II period. A large rock-cut cistern, located 5m outside the SW corner of the fortress, dated to the 9th-7th century BCE. It has a heart-shaped plan, measuring 11.95x7.7m with a current depth of 1.7m (estimated original 4m), and an estimated volume of 250 cubic meters. It features a square opening and two layers of plaster, collecting runoff from the fortress and surrounding areas, possibly supplemented by a nearby spring.

Name: Khirbet Abu Tabaq (Kerem Atrad) (ח'רבת אבו טבק (כרם עטרד))
Description: The Abu Tabaq Cave, located at the foot of the fortress, served as a reservoir. It is 35m long, 7m wide, and 5m high, with a built entrance and steps leading inside. A rock-cut cistern, 18m from the Abu Tabaq Cave, approximately 6m deep with a 1m diameter opening. It is located beneath the fortress, suggesting a shaft for drawing water from within the fortification.

Name: Khirbet Bint-Barr (חורבת בנת בר)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Bannat Bar, dated to the Iron Age II period. A rectangular plastered cistern (approx. 4x3m, 3.5m deep, 40 cubic meters) with Iron Age plaster, and two bell-shaped cisterns (one 3.5m diameter/depth, 23 cubic meters; another 6m diameter, 3m deep, 56 cubic meters) were identified, dating to the 8th century BCE.

Name: Khirbet Deir es-Sidd (חורבת דיר א-סיד)
Description: Rock-cut cisterns with channels leading to them were found on the steep slopes of this extensive settlement. These cisterns were used during the Iron Age II and continued into the Second Temple period. Cisterns or pools were found at Deir es-Sid, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Khirbet el-Khuwwakh (Etam) (ח'רבת אל-ח'וואח (עיטם))
Description: A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Ayyats during the Iron Age II. A large natural karstic cave, 42m long, 4m wide, and 2m high, with an estimated capacity of 300 cubic meters. It was plastered with two layers of plaster dating to Iron Age II, indicating its use as a water reservoir, with an entrance for drawing water and another for collecting runoff or spring water. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city.

Name: Khirbet el-Mekari (ח'רבת אל-מקארי)
Description: Two adjacent rock-cut cisterns at Ma'aghir et-Tabaqa, 200m NW of the fortress. They measure 13x8m and 15x8m, with depths of 3-4m, and likely served the Iron Age II settlement.

Name: Khirbet Halukim (חורבת חלוקים)
Description: Two open cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands. One cistern has a volume of approximately 300 cubic meters.

Name: Khirbet Marjameh (חורבת מרג'מה)
Description: A rock-cut cistern opening was found near the 8th-century BCE fortifications, though its size and plaster type are unknown. The primary water source for the city was the large Ein Samia spring nearby. Cisterns or pools were found at Qala' Marjama, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Khirbet Meshura (חורבת משורה)
Description: Three rock-cut cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to store water.

Name: Khirbet Raddana (חורבת רדנה)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Khirbet Raddana, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Khirbet Rahba (חורבת רחבה)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water. Two rock-cut cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to store water.

Name: Khirbet Ramat Boker (חורבת רמת בוקר)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Khirbet Ratama (חורבת רתמה)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Khirbet Tov (חורבת טוב)
Description: A fortress from the 7th century BCE with a water system comprising a well (3.9m diameter and depth) located 46m from the fortress, and a channel passing through the fortress wall, likely for collecting runoff and possibly supplemented by the well. An unlocated water reservoir within the fortress is hypothesized. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. Wells were found at Khirbet Tov, which are dated with high probability to the Iron Age II period. A reservoir with an external feeding system was possibly identified at Khirbet Tov during the Iron Age II, though its identification is noted with some uncertainty.

Name: Midas City (מידאס סיטי (פריגיה))
Description: A fortified city with several tunnels and stepped passages cut into the rock, leading to springs below the city level. These systems, including a large cave-like chamber with ventilation shafts and a fountain, provided hidden access to water during sieges. A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Midas City, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Migdal Nahal Sarapid (מגדל נחל סרפד)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Mishor Haruach (מישור הרוח)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Mitzad Nahal Akrav (מצודת נחל עקרב)
Description: One open cistern (possibly two), part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Mitzad Nahal Boker (מצד נחל בוקר)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water. Two rock-cut cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to store water.

Name: Mitzad Nahal Ela (מצד נחל אלה)
Description: Two open cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Mitzad Nahal Tzana (מצד נחל צנע)
Description: Four open cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water.

Name: Mitzad Sarapid (מצד סרפד)
Description: One open cistern, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to collect runoff water. Two rock-cut cisterns, part of the Iron Age II water supply in the Negev Highlands, designed to store water.

Name: Mycenae (מיקנה (יוון))
Description: A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Mycenae, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Nessana (נצנה)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Nessana, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Nimrud (Kalhu) (נמרוד (כלח))
Description: Three deep wells were found in the Northwest Palace of Ashurnasirpal II (884-859 BCE). The well in room NN was 25.4m deep and lined with bricks, used for about 250 years, while others were found in courtyard AJ and room AB. An aqueduct, about 28 km long, was built by Ashurnasirpal II (884-859 BCE) to bring water from the Great Zab river to Nimrud. It included the Negub Tunnel, a rock-cut tunnel with shafts, which diverted water through a ridge, and is considered the oldest aqueduct in the world. An aqueduct bringing water from a distance outside the city was found at Nimrud, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Nineveh (נינוה (אשור))
Description: Sennacherib (704-681 BCE) built extensive water systems for Nineveh, including the Kisiri Canal (16km) from the Khosr river, diverting 18 streams from the Bashiqah mountains, and the Hinis Canal (55km) from the Gomel river basin, which crossed rivers via bridges (like Jerwan) and mountains via tunnels. An Assyrian relief from the time of Ashurbanipal (668-631 BCE) depicts an aqueduct on pointed arches, similar to the Jerwan aqueduct built by Sennacherib, bringing water to a flourishing garden near Nineveh. An aqueduct bringing water from a distance outside the city was found at Nineveh, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Qumran (קומראן)
Description: A unique round cistern (Locus 110), 6.5m deep with a diameter of 5.05-5.3m, and a volume of 136 cubic meters. It features a 70cm thick wall with four layers of plaster and an inlet channel 0.85m below the rim, which functioned during Iron Age II. Cisterns or pools were found at Qumran, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Samos (Eupalinos Tunnel) (מנהרת אופלינוס (סמוס))
Description: The Eupalinos Tunnel, built in the 6th century BCE, is a 1040m long tunnel cut through a mountain to supply water from a spring to the city of Samos. It included an initial 890m covered aqueduct section, vertical shafts, and a complex rock-cut tunnel with a deep trench for water pipes, demonstrating advanced engineering. An aqueduct bringing water from a distance outside the city was found at Samos, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Tel Arad (תל ערד)
Description: A water system for the fortress, including a deep well (25.19m deep, 4.6m diameter) outside the walls, and a covered rock-cut channel (24m long) leading under the city wall to three large plastered cisterns (approx. 250 cubic meters) inside the fortress. The system collected runoff and was supplemented by water from the well. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. Wells were found at Tel Arad, which are dated with high probability to the Iron Age II period. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Tel Arad during the Iron Age II.

Name: Tel Aroer (תל ערוער)
Description: A walled settlement from the 7th century BCE with a large, unexcavated, bowl-shaped depression (40m diameter, 6m deep) within the walls, hypothesized to be a subterranean water reservoir fed by floodwaters from Nahal Aroer. Additionally, wells outside the settlement were likely used. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A well was found at Tel Aroer, dated to the Iron Age II period. A reservoir with an external feeding system was possibly identified at Tel Aroer during the Iron Age II, though its identification is noted with some uncertainty.

Name: Tel Ashdod (תל אשדוד)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Ashdod, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Azekah (תל עזקה)
Description: An Assyrian inscription (Azekah Inscription) from Sargon II's campaign (712 BCE) mentions 'water' and 'canal' in the context of conquering a city, possibly hinting at the use or destruction of a water system, or a siege tactic involving a water tunnel.

Name: Tel Beersheba (תל באר שבע)
Description: An elaborate internal city water system from Iron Age II, consisting of a deep entrance shaft, a large double-cruciform plastered reservoir (approx. 500 cubic meters) fed by floodwaters from Nahal Hebron via a channel, and a deep well outside the city walls (Iron Age I, but used in Iron Age II). Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, specifically mentioning a cruciform-shaped reservoir designed to maximize storage volume and prevent roof collapse. Wells were found at Tel Beersheba, including three associated with 'Nimrod', dating to the Iron Age II period. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Tel Beersheba during the Iron Age II.

Name: Tel Beit Mirsim (תל בית מרסים)
Description: Several cisterns were found in Layer A (Iron Age II). One in the SE area (338-15) was 6m deep, with a built and rock-cut section, and a well-preserved, plastered channel leading to it from the NE, likely draining roofs. A settling basin was present at the channel's entry point. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Beit Mirsim, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Beit Shemesh (תל בית שמש)
Description: A monumental, cruciform-shaped rock-cut reservoir (24x23.5m, 6m high) in Area C, fed by multiple channels collecting runoff, was constructed in the 10th century BCE (Iron IIA) and reused in the 7th century BCE. A round cistern in Area B, dated to Iron Age II, measuring 5.75m in diameter and 7m deep. It features a 0.6m diameter opening, a 5m neck (3m built, 2m rock-cut), and 10cm thick gray plaster. Its estimated volume is 87 cubic meters. A rock-cut, spherical cistern in Area A, dated to Iron Age II, with a 1x1m square opening and a 1.5m neck, reaching a depth of 4.5m. Its volume is approximately 15 cubic meters (excluding the neck), with traces of disintegrated plaster found. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, specifically mentioning a cruciform-shaped reservoir designed to maximize storage volume and prevent roof collapse. A reservoir or pool was found at Tel Beit Shemesh, dated to the Iron Age II period. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Beit Shemesh, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel en-Nasbeh (תל א-נצבה)
Description: The site contains numerous water cisterns, distinguished from granaries by their waterproof plaster, indicating their function for water storage during Iron Age II.

Name: Tel Gerisa (תל גריסה)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Gerisa, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Gezer (תל גזר)
Description: A large, double rock-cut reservoir, approximately 18m deep with plastered walls, was likely filled by runoff water. The excavator dates this installation to the Iron Age. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A reservoir or pool was found at Tel Gezer, dated to the Iron Age II period. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Gezer, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Halif (תל חליף)
Description: A rectangular, well-plastered cistern, measuring 9x4x3.5m, was uncovered in Area IV. It is dated to the Iron Age II period. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Halif, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Hazor (תל חצור)
Description: A large, complex water system was constructed in the 10th-9th century BCE (Iron Age IIA) in the southwestern corner of the tel. It consists of an entrance, a deep shaft (approx. 30m), and a 25m long tunnel leading to the underground water table, designed to secure water supply during sieges. Mentioned as a site with an underground water system where a pulley could have been used, similar to the one depicted in an Assyrian relief, suggesting a sophisticated water supply during sieges. A well was found at Tel Hazor, dated to the Iron Age II period. Cisterns or pools were possibly identified at Tel Hazor during the Iron Age II, though their identification is noted with some uncertainty. A major water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Tel Hazor, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Tel Ira (תל עירא)
Description: Six cisterns were found within the city, dating to the 8th-7th century BCE. They feature rock-cut necks and rims protected by four large stone slabs. These cisterns were the sole local water supply for the city.

Name: Tel Jezreel (תל יזרעאל)
Description: The site utilized numerous rock-cut, plastered cisterns (dozens to hundreds, with two dated to Iron Age II having capacities of 36 and 56 cubic meters) for rainwater collection, supplemented by the Ein Jezreel spring (Ein el-Meiyiteh) which was also used during droughts. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Jezreel, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Lachish (תל לכיש)
Description: The deep well (44m deep) originally constructed in the Middle Bronze Age continued to serve as a primary water source for the city during Iron II. It is proposed that a runoff water reservoir, similar to those at Beit Shemesh or Beersheba, existed in the northern part of the tel to provide an additional water source for the city during Iron II, though its exact location and completion are debated. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A well was found at Tel Lachish, dated to the Iron Age II period. A reservoir or pool, possibly for water storage, was identified at Tel Lachish during the Iron Age II, though its identification is noted with some uncertainty.

Name: Tel Megiddo (תל מגידו)
Description: Megiddo features a complex water system with two main phases. The 'gallery' (secret passage) providing access to a natural cave and well is dated by Yadin to the 10th century BCE (Iron Age IIA). A later, monumental system, also from Iron Age II, includes a large shaft (36m deep) and a 50m long tunnel, constructed to access the same water source from within the city walls. Megiddo's impressive water system, consisting of a pit and a tunnel, is attributed by the author and most scholars to Iron Age II. A plastered reservoir with a monumental staircase, located outside the outer gate (Locus 2153), was supplied by the nearby Ein Kubi spring or collected runoff. It is dated to the time of Ahab (Iron II). Mentioned as a site with an underground water system where a pulley could have been used, similar to the one depicted in an Assyrian relief, suggesting a sophisticated water supply during sieges. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with three monumental water systems, likely involving tunnels or shafts to access groundwater within the fortified city. A major water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Tel Megiddo, dating to the Iron Age II. A reservoir with an external feeding system was identified at Tel Megiddo during the Iron Age II.

Name: Tel Shiloh (תל שילה)
Description: Cisterns or pools were found at Shiloh, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Taanach (תל תענך)
Description: Mentioned as having an underground water system (from the Late Bronze Age) that provides a comparison for the type of system depicted in the Assyrian relief, implying its continued relevance or similar design in Iron Age II. Cisterns or pools were found at Tel Taanach, dated to the Iron Age II period.

Name: Tel Yokneam (תל יקנעם)
Description: A proposed water system, similar to Hazor's, is indicated by an oval-shaped pit carved into the rock in the lowest part of the city, near external springs. The city's casemate wall, built in the 10th century BCE (Iron Age IIA), incorporates this feature, suggesting a shaft leading to groundwater. Listed as one of 17 sites in Iron Age II Israel with a monumental water system, likely involving a tunnel or shaft to access groundwater within the fortified city. A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Tel Yokneam, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Tiryns (טירינס (יוון))
Description: A water system, cut to a spring or groundwater within the fortified city, was found at Tiryns, dating to the Iron Age II.

Name: Toprakkale (Rusahinili) (טופראק קלה (רוסהינילי))
Description: An aqueduct bringing water from a distance outside the city was found at Toprakkale, dating to the Iron Age II. Around 700 BCE, King Rusa I or II created artificial Lake Rusa by building dams at Kesis Goli and diverting water from the Aliyani river to supply the new capital Toprakkale (Rusahinili) and its gardens. Lake Sihke was used to regulate the water flow.

Name: Tushpa / Menua Canal (Van) (תושפה / אמת מנואה (אוררטו))
Description: The 'Mena's Canal' (Manua's Canal), a 56 km long aqueduct built by King Manua (805-785 BCE), supplied water from the Engil river spring to Tushpa, overcoming the non-potable Lake Van water. It included stone dams, channels, and support walls up to 20m high, operating for 2500 years.

Name: Ulhu (אולחו)
Description: An irrigation system around Ulhu, including a main aqueduct and numerous qanats (underground channels) dug from the mountain, was destroyed by King Sargon II of Assyria (722-705 BCE). This is the earliest textual evidence of qanats in Urartu.

Name: Umm el-Biyara (אום אל-ביארה)
Description: Eight bell-shaped, rock-cut cisterns, located at the lowest point of the plateau to collect runoff. They have round openings (~90cm), are ~4m deep, and are plastered with strong light gray-white plaster. One cistern has an inlet channel, and each has a volume of ~33 cubic meters. Cisterns or pools were found at Umm el-Biyara, dated to the Iron Age II period.
